body:
News
                In addition to declining funding, the survey identified a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns and financial precarity.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            A new report tracks the challenges facing publications that cover arts and culture. (edit Valentina Di Liscia/Hyperallergic, image KC Green)Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week. The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

title: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
description:
News
                The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would speed up permitting for major projects and could i
body:
News
                The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would speed up permitting for major projects and could impact Indigenous sovereignty over culturally significant land. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Fence leading to uranium mine near Mount Taylor in New Mexico (photo Eve Andree Laramee courtesy Netherzone via Wikimedia Commons CC-BY-SA-4.0)
    
        
            Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites. The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.

title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
description:
Book Review
                Taking David Hockney’s painting of arts patron Betty Freeman as his subject, James Cahill tells the
body:
Book Review
                Taking David Hockney’s painting of arts patron Betty Freeman as his subject, James Cahill tells the engrossing story of two friends who shaped the cultural landscape of 1960s Los Angeles.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            David Hockney and Betty Freeman at Freeman's house in 1967 with "Beverly Hills Housewife" (photo John Kasmin, courtesy the artist and Lyndsey Ingram)
    
        
            In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.David Hockney and Betty Freeman at Freeman's home on November 15, 1987 (image courtesy Special Collections & Archives, UC San Diego Library)

body:
Art Fairs
                The Art Dealers Association of America’s chummy five-day show returns to the Upper East Side after quietly canceling last fall’s edition.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Gallerist David Lusk with Greely Myatt‘s speech-bubble artworks at the ADAA fair (all photos Aaron Short/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA). “We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic. “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview. Works by Masako Miki on view at the ADAA

title: Special Edition: Jesus
description:

                Mona Chalabi, Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang, Miles Greenberg, Betsy James Wyeth, and the ho
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Mona Chalabi, Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang, Miles Greenberg, Betsy James Wyeth, and the hottest memes about the Nvidia honeypot.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.  In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago. Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.    And then I see her. She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
		
	
	
		“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). |  Lakshmi Rivera Amin

title: Former Philadelphia Museum of Art Executive Charged $30K to Company Cards
description: A former Philadelphia Museum of Art executive admitted on Friday to using company credit cards to make approximately $30,000 in personal purchases,
body:
A former Philadelphia Museum of Art executive admitted on Friday to using company credit cards to make approximately $30,000 in personal purchases, the Inquirer reports.

	Latasha Harling, the museum’s former chief people and diversity officer, pleaded guilty to receiving stolen property, averting a trial that had been scheduled for Friday.

	Common Pleas Court Judge Leon King II sentenced Harling, 44, to five years of probation for the misdemeanor offense. King also ordered her to pay the museum $30,000 in restitution in monthly installments of at least $500, beginning in January. If she pays the full amount before her probation ends, however, Harling may request early termination of her probation.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Harling joined the museum in November 2023 as its inaugural chief people officer (CPO), overseeing human resources and diversity initiatives. Her budgetary responsibilities, the Inquirer noted, included access to corporate credit cards. An affidavit of probable cause filed in connection with her arrest recounts how museum officials grew suspicious of her activities in January 2025, after being alerted to a series of significant, seemingly personal purchases on her credit card statements. A subsequent audit by the museum’s chief financial officer found that Harling had charged $58,885 in personal expenses to the card since her hiring.

	Harling was offered the opportunity to repay $32,565 to the museum, the affidavit states. She resigned shortly thereafter, with the credit card expenses still outstanding. The museum then sought to recover the money: The following February, Harling signed a promissory note agreeing to repay $19,380 over three months. After receiving no payments by April, the museum contacted police.

	A spokesperson for the museum said in a statement that its officials are “grateful that the case” is resolved and that “we look forward to returning our focus to the exhibitions, programs, and experiences we provide for our community.”

title: ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger

body:
Recognizing an influential living artist having a retrospective or survey exhibition at a major US museum.

	Maren Hassinger for “Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (June 6–November 29, 2026)

	For five decades, Maren Hassinger has been making elegant, spare sculptures that have enlisted a diverse array of materials, from wire rope to pink plastic bags to newspaper to rose leaves. The objects she incorporates in her art are the kind that could easily be bent, twisted, or broken. In another setting, they might even be seen as flimsy. But Hassinger sculpts them in a way where they appear firm, monumental, and alive. Across an oeuvre that has included installations, performances, films, drawings, and more, Hassinger has repeatedly returned to the concept of motion, imbuing static objects with a sense of movement, as if they are shifting before our eyes. Frequently, she does so by referring to the natural environment, invoking trees and water with works that appear to undulate because of the way they are installed.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Her retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, billed as the most expansive show of her art to date, positioned her as a key figure in the transition away from Minimalism. During the 1970s, Hassinger began working with wire rope that she partially pulled apart. The use of a material associated with industry synched with a tendency seen at the time in New York, where a range of sculptors transformed steel, firebricks, and fluorescent lights into large and often heavy artworks. Hassinger’s approach differed in its overt allusions to the human body and its intentionally light touch. While Hassinger’s collaborations with artists like Senga Nengudi and Ulysses Jenkins are now well-known, the BAMPFA show put forward Hassinger as a performance artist in her own right, noting that she sought to become a dancer before settling on sculpture during her education. Her sculptures would go on to translate those choreographies, which could not be permanently viewable within gallery spaces.

	The concept of ephemerality has also been core to Hassinger’s body of work, and the BAMPFA show highlighted it prominently by featuring her works that make use of pink plastic bags or old newspapers, objects that might easily be thrown in the trash but that Hassinger sees as worthy art materials. Ranging from large-scale installations to intimate weavings, she always seeks to make beauty of what could easily be treated as refuse. In the BAMPFA catalog, speaking to curator Lowery Stokes Sims of the newspaper pieces, Hassinger says, “Well I don’t want to look at something ugly. I want things to be as finished and pleasant as possible. And why not?”
	

	Nominees:

	Coco Fusco“Coco Fusco: Tomorrow, I Will Become an Island” at El Museo del Barrio, New York (September 18, 2025–March 1, 2026)

	Suzanne Jackson“Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love” at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (September 27, 2025–March 1, 2026); traveled to the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis (May 14–August 23, 2026) and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (September 26, 2026–January 18, 2027)

	David Lamelas“David Lamelas: The Machine” at Dia Chelsea, New York (March 6, 2026–January 16, 2027)

	Martin Puryear“Martin Puryear: Nexus” at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (September 27, 2025–February 8, 2026); traveled to the Cleveland Museum of Art (April 12, 2026–August 9, 2026)
